ideas.title: Copper wire that remembers every bend
ideas.nearest: Chipping a stone to change its note
ideas.critique: A plastic elastic rod with springback, work hardening and a fatigue snap has a direct real-world counterpart in the paper clip. That makes it new physics for the island, and the player learns from it that they have to over-bend. Material that keeps its mark, then gets used as a hook that holds the lantern, is the big goal made literal. The risks are a beak that grips and twists at the aimed point, which is a hard control problem, and a fatigue counter that reads as a hidden timer rather than a wire that visibly tires.

ideas.title: Centre the clay or it wobbles
ideas.critique: A full 3D viscoplastic MPM body answers round 2's objection that a shell of revolution can only squash evenly: off-centre mass and one-sided folding are what it can do. But a spinning MPM clay body pushed by a finger in real time is a very large build. The most likely version is a slow offline solve, or a wobble that is one parameter, and then the kick wheel the player throws on becomes a film they watch.

ideas.title: Candles dipped layer by layer
ideas.critique: Drag-out thickness per dip and frozen drips are an honest record of the making, and a candle that lights the cottage is a real use. But the payoff film is a third hot-material glow lighting its surroundings at night, right after the glass still. Repeated dipping is also a slow loop with one dial, and the burning-down by its own shape is the hard part, the one most likely to become a shrinking cylinder.

ideas.title: The chisel bites the spinning log
ideas.critique: This is round 2's idea again, reworded, and the verdict stands: the cutting force, the sagging torque and the kickback are what make it a chisel. Since the last post was a failed tops film, this is the project's retake. It only surprises if the catch and the slowing lathe are felt in play and read clearly in a film where the camera actually sees the lathe.
